title: Belgrade Grows Distant: Milošević Signals Exhaustion
sources: ICTY Martić Trial Judgment (IT-95-11-T), Serbia–RSK–RS coordination findings
content:
By the late summer of 1993, the calculus in Belgrade had begun to shift. The Vance-Owen Plan had collapsed on the Bosnian Serb assembly’s rejection, and its successor, the Owen-Stoltenberg “Union of Three Republics,” was on the table. Serbia under Slobodan Milošević was by now deep in the grip of the comprehensive sanctions tightened by UN Security Council Resolution 820 (1993): hyperinflation was destroying the dinar, fuel was scarce, and the economic cost of underwriting two Serb war efforts — in Bosnia and in the Croatian Krajina — was becoming unsustainable. Milošević began to signal exhaustion, distancing Belgrade from the maximalist positions of the Pale leadership.

This distancing was not a moral conversion but a strategic recalculation. Milošević’s overriding aim had narrowed to relief from sanctions and the rehabilitation of Serbia’s international position; the territorial ambitions of the Bosnian Serbs were increasingly a liability to that aim. The ICTY Martić Trial Judgment (IT-95-11-T), addressing the wider architecture of Serbian coordination across the Republika Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska, documented how decisions taken in Belgrade shaped the room for manoeuvre of the dependent Serb leaderships — and how Belgrade could withdraw cover when its own interests required.

For the Pale leadership, a patron signalling exhaustion was a graver problem than a patron issuing orders. An order could be defied at a contained cost; a sponsor losing the will to sustain the war threatened the material basis of the entire project. The distancing that began in 1993 foreshadowed the open rupture of 1994, when Belgrade would formally close the border to all but humanitarian traffic.

The decision facing the leadership was whether to read Belgrade’s fatigue as a warning to be heeded or as a bluff to be resisted. To acknowledge the signal was to begin adjusting war aims toward what the patron could still underwrite. To resist it was to gamble that Belgrade’s commitment would outlast its complaints — a gamble whose terms grew worse with every month of sanctions.
